headline: High risk: OpenHands can ingest LangGraph outputs into writable runtimes, creating dangerous default-path prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading action errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LangGraph is a library with application-defined files and broad egress; OpenHands runs an agent loop with shell/browser/editor and MCP support. If LangGraph outputs are passed into OpenHands via files or runtime inputs, attacker-controlled content can be treated as instructions. The shared path is plausible but not proven by docs alone.
conditions: IF LangGraph writes untrusted content into files that OpenHands later reads as prompts or tasks
IF the two are connected through a shared mounted workspace or runtime input channel
mitigations: Add a strict prompt/content delimiter before OpenHands consumes LangGraph output
Review and sanitize any file-based handoff between the agents
Disable automatic task ingestion from shared files
Use separate workspaces for each agent
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad filesystem read/write and broad network egress. LangGraph touches application-defined graph state and OpenHands reads files mounted into its runtime, so shared workspace data can flow into model-provider calls. This creates a realistic leakage path for secrets or sensitive work products in default-style deployments.
conditions: IF both agents access the same mounted workspace or checkpointer-backed state
IF either agent forwards file contents or state into a model provider call
mitigations: Separate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces
Restrict which files each agent may read
Redact secrets before any model call
Turn off shared checkpointer/state for sensitive runs
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LangGraph can write filesystem state and OpenHands can write files, modify git state, install packages, and use MCP. In a shared directory or repo, both can mutate the same resources without any locking guarantee in the profiles, so concurrent writes and git-state corruption are plausible and potentially destructive.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem path or git repository
IF no external lock or serialization layer is added by the orchestrator
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory
Serialize write access with a lock file
Avoid concurrent git operations
Pause one agent while the other mutates shared state
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: LangGraph is an orchestration framework whose outputs can become downstream inputs, while OpenHands is an action-taking coding agent with shell and browser tools. If OpenHands treats LangGraph-produced plans, facts, or code as authoritative, a single upstream mistake can cascade into commits, shell actions, or browser-driven side effects.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes LangGraph output without an explicit verification step
IF that output is used to trigger shell commands, browser actions, or code changes
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Insert a verification step between agents
Limit OpenHands to read-only mode for handoffs
Use structured outputs with schema validation
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking before action execution

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and the listed data classes are application files or graph state, so no specific residency or regulated-data mismatch is evidenced. I do not cite only one agent because the compliance question here is about the pair's shared handling of ordinary workspace data, and the profiles do not show a jurisdictional conflict.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace
IF one deployment adds retention or residency constraints not reflected in these profiles
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Document retention settings for both runtimes
Use separate storage for sensitive projects
Review vendor/data-processing terms before deployment
